title: The Professional Learning Revolution
author: Adam Kohlbeck
summary: Adam Kohlbeck reviews Stuart Kime and Rob Coe's paper 'We need a revolution in professional learning', which argues that teacher professional learning should be a protected priority, should build expertise, and should be evaluated for whether it works. He values the paper as a conversation starter that grounds decisions in evidence while leaving context to drive design, rather than a prescription. He then applies two of its critiques to coaching, focusing on the charge that professional learning is too often generic. He argues that schools pursue consistency of action when they should pursue consistency of understanding, since teaching is a complex system where decision-making matters more than identical moves. He warns that evaluating the presence of a technique breeds compliance, and that one-to-one coaching can still be generic when it follows a playbook. His remedy is to co-construct the teacher's real problem of practice before choosing a technique, illustrated by a Think, Pair, Share lesson where shallow answers were reframed as a problem of driving student thinking.
points: Kohlbeck reads the Kime and Coe paper as a conversation starter that offers evidence as underpinning for design decisions, not a template of what to do next week.
He distinguishes consistency of action from consistency of understanding, arguing that shared mental models of how learning works support better teacher decisions in an uncertain classroom.
Evaluating whether a technique is present, or prescribing both problem and solution, closes down the reflective collegiate talk that schools say they want.
One-to-one coaching can still be generic if every coach works through the same playbook, so coaches should co-construct the teacher's actual problem of practice first.
A Think, Pair, Share example shows how turning a single weak answer into a recurring problem of driving student thinking led to a technique fitted to that teacher.
quotes: This paper pushes readers to see the evidence as an underpinning for their decision-making around professional learning design; their context is the driver for those design decisions.
If we evaluate the presence of a specific technique or strategy as a sign of success or otherwise, no one is going to think much further than compliance.

If a teacher has the problem prescribed to them (students not having attention secured before teaching begins) and then also has the solution prescribed (using a 3,2,1 countdown), I don’t hold out much hope for lots of collegiate discussion because there simply isn’t space for it.
we would be better served in developing consistency of understanding that fuels the mental models that guide the decision-making of teachers.
This incentivises teachers to focus on visual implementation of the most ‘doable’ technique or strategy that has been discussed in the session.
A one-to-one coaching conversation can still be very generic. For example, a coach could go from session to session working with teachers one at a time on the same technique or sets of techniques.
for coaching to overcome the genericism problem, it needs to allow space for the teacher and coach to con-construct what the problem actually looks and feels like for that teacher.
